Hail damage: what Fort Worth homeowners should check first

August 27, 2026 · 6 min read · Fort Worth, TX

It is 9:40 pm on a spring Tuesday in Fort Worth and the hail has just stopped. Your phone is lighting up with neighborhood group posts, the dog is still hiding under the bed, and you are standing at the back door with a flashlight wondering whether that racket on the roof was expensive or just loud. Every hail season we meet homeowners in exactly that moment, and the honest answer is that you cannot tell from the back porch. But you can learn a lot in the next fifteen minutes without ever touching a ladder, and what you check first determines whether damage gets documented while it is fresh or discovered two years later as a stained ceiling.

Start on the ground, not the roof

Do not climb up after a storm. Wet shingles are slick, hail-bruised shingles are fragile, and nothing on that roof is worth an emergency room visit. Walk the property instead. The soft metals around your house record hail like a black box: gutters, downspouts, the fins on the AC condenser, mailbox tops, window screens, and any aluminum fascia. If the hail was large enough to bruise composition shingles, it almost always left dimples in these softer surfaces first.

Check the driveway and patio for shingle granules. A little granule wash after heavy rain is normal, especially on older roofs. Piles of granules at the downspout exits right after a hail event are not. That grit is your roof's sun protection washing into the yard.

What hail damage actually looks like on shingles

On composition shingles, which cover the large majority of Fort Worth homes, hail strikes rarely look dramatic. There is usually no hole, no missing shingle, nothing a drone photo from the street will show. What an inspector looks for up close:

  • Round dark bruises where granules were knocked loose, often soft to the touch like a bruised apple
  • Cracked or dented ridge caps, which sit highest and take hits first
  • Dents in roof vents, flashing, skylights, and rubber pipe boots
  • Exposed black fiberglass mat on older, brittle shingles

Why the ridge line tells the truth

Ridge caps face the sky at the flattest angle, so they absorb the most direct impact. When we inspect after a Tarrant County storm, the ridge is usually where the story is clearest. If the caps are clean, the field of the roof often held up too. If the caps are cracked and bruised, the slopes that faced the storm deserve a shingle-by-shingle look.

Why waiting is the expensive move

A bruised shingle does not leak on day one. It loses its granules, bakes under the Texas heat cycle through July and August, dries out, and cracks over the following seasons. By the time water reaches the decking, the connection to that spring storm is much harder to establish, and the repair has grown from shingles to decking and sometimes drywall. This matters for insurance too. Most policies set time limits for reporting storm damage, and the Texas Department of Insurance publishes plain-language guides on how the claim process works. We are not adjusters and we do not promise outcomes: we document what is on the roof with photos, and your adjuster decides. But an adjuster can only work with evidence, and evidence is easiest to capture while the damage is fresh.

There is also a practical scheduling reality. After a widespread hail event, every reputable crew in the metroplex books out fast, so the sooner your roof is looked at, the sooner you know whether you need a spot on anyone's schedule at all. If it turns out you do need a full replacement, it helps to know how long a roof replacement actually takes before the calendar fills.

Practical tip: Before storm season even starts, take dated photos of your gutters, downspouts, AC unit, and each side of the house from the ground, then repeat the same photos after any hailstorm. Ten minutes of pictures gives you a clean before-and-after record that removes all guesswork later.

Watch out for the storm-chaser knock

Within 48 hours of any decent hail event, out-of-town crews start canvassing Fort Worth neighborhoods with clipboards and urgency. Some are legitimate. Many are not, and the bad ones share a script: your roof is definitely totaled, sign today, they will handle everything. A local company with a Tarrant County address and local references has to stand behind its work for years, not until the next storm system three states away. Take the flyer if you want, but get a second opinion from someone who will still be here in October.

Get it documented by someone local

A proper post-storm inspection covers every slope, the ridge, the soft metals, the penetrations, and the attic if there is any sign of moisture. We photograph everything and give you a straight answer, including the answer that your roof is fine, which is genuinely how a good share of these inspections end. We run these across the area, including free storm inspections in Saginaw for neighborhoods north of Fort Worth that sit right in the usual storm track.

If your street took hail this spring and nobody has put eyes on your roof yet, get it looked at before summer bakes the evidence. And once this storm is behind you, it is worth knowing the signs a roof needs attention before fall storm season so the next front does not catch the same weak spots.

Common questions

Can hail damage exist even if I see no leaks?
Yes, and it usually does at first. Hail bruising shortens the life of the shingle long before water gets through. Most hail-damaged roofs we inspect have zero interior symptoms on day one.
How soon after a storm should I get an inspection?
Within a few weeks is ideal. Fresh damage is easier to identify, and most insurance policies have time limits for reporting storm damage, so earlier documentation protects your options.
Will you tell me if my roof is actually fine?
Yes. A good portion of our post-storm inspections end with us telling the homeowner their roof held up. We would rather earn your trust for the storm that does get you than sell you work you do not need.

Think your roof took a hit?

Get a free, documented hail inspection from a Fort Worth crew that will give you a straight answer either way.

How long does a roof replacement actually take?

August 20, 2026 · 6 min read · Fort Worth, TX

The quote is sitting on your kitchen table, the number is circled, and the question your spouse actually asks first has nothing to do with money: how long is this going to take, and how bad will it be while it happens? Fair question. The honest answer for most Fort Worth homes is that the tear-off and install itself typically takes one to two days. The full journey from signed agreement to the crew driving away is usually one to three weeks, and most of that gap is scheduling and materials, not work on your roof. Here is the whole timeline the way we walk clients through it, including the parts that can stretch.

Before a single shingle comes off

Once you sign, three things happen in parallel. Materials get ordered, and common architectural shingles are usually available from DFW suppliers within days, while specialty colors, Class 4 impact-rated products, or metal panels can add a week or more. Your job gets a slot on the install calendar. And any required permitting gets handled, which varies by city; Fort Worth and the surrounding Tarrant County towns each run their own process, and we handle that paperwork so you do not have to.

This pre-work window is also when material decisions get finalized. If you are still weighing options, our breakdown of shingle versus metal costs covers how we frame that choice at the kitchen table.

Install day, hour by hour

For a typical single-story home in the 2,000 to 2,500 square foot range, expect roughly this rhythm:

  • 7 to 8 am: crew arrives, tarps go down over landscaping, pools, and AC units
  • Morning: full tear-off down to the deck, damaged decking flagged and replaced
  • Midday: underlayment, ice and water barrier in the valleys, drip edge, flashing
  • Afternoon: shingles, ridge vents, pipe boots, ridge caps
  • End of day: magnet sweep for nails, debris hauled off, walkthrough with you

Larger homes, steep pitches, multiple layers of old shingles, or decking surprises push this to two or occasionally three days. Metal roofs generally take two to four days because panel work is slower and more precise. Two-story homes add staging time simply because everything travels farther.

Expect noise. Tear-off and nailing shake the whole house, and there is no quiet version of this work. Most homeowners in Fort Worth plan a normal workday away from the house, send pets to a friend or a daycare for the day, and warn any work-from-home neighbors. The crew needs power, a clear driveway, and a number where they can reach you if a decking decision comes up. That is the entire homeowner job description on install day.

What can stretch the timeline

Weather

We do not tear off with rain in the near forecast, period. North Texas can produce a surprise line of storms in almost any month, and the spring hail window and the fall front season both force reschedules. A weather delay is annoying; an open roof deck in a thunderstorm is a disaster. If radar turns on us mid-job, the exposed deck gets dried in with synthetic underlayment before the crew leaves, every time.

Decking

Nobody knows the true condition of the wood under your shingles until the tear-off exposes it. Most homes need a handful of boards replaced. Occasionally an older home with a history of slow leaks needs significantly more, and that can add a day. We photograph any decking we replace and show you before it gets covered, so the change order is never a mystery.

After the last shingle

We finish with a final quality inspection, a second magnet sweep of the yard and driveway, debris haul-off, and your warranty registration. Manufacturer warranties on the shingles and our workmanship warranty both get documented in writing, following the installation standards the National Roofing Contractors Association publishes. If anything looks off in the weeks after, from a scuffed gutter to a shingle that did not seat, one call brings us back.

Practical tip: The day before install, move cars out of the garage and driveway, take fragile items off interior walls and shelves, and mark sprinkler heads with flags. Tear-off vibration is real, and the crew cannot protect what they cannot see.

The Tarrant County scheduling reality

One more timing note for local homeowners: after a major hail event, every crew in the metroplex books up at once, and lead times that are normally a week or two can stretch to a month or more. If your roof took damage in a spring storm, getting inspected and on a calendar early matters more than any other factor you control. Our guide to checking your roof after hail covers what to look for before you ever call anyone.

Timelines also shift a little between cities because of permitting and inspection differences. If you are west of Fort Worth, we keep a page on roof replacement in White Settlement with the local specifics.

The short version: plan for one loud day, maybe two. Plan for a week or three of lead time. And if a roofer promises you a date without asking about your decking, your pitch, or the forecast, treat the promise accordingly.

Common questions

Do I need to be home during the install?
No. Most homeowners work a normal day. We need access to power, a clear driveway, and a phone number where we can reach you if a decking decision comes up.
How loud is it, and what about pets?
Loud. Tear-off and nailing shake the house all day. Many homeowners arrange for dogs and cats to spend install day elsewhere, and anyone working from home should plan around it.
What happens if it rains mid-project?
We watch forecasts closely and do not open more roof than we can dry-in the same day. If weather moves in, the exposed deck gets synthetic underlayment or tarps before the crew leaves. Your home is never left open overnight.

Shingle vs metal: honest cost math for Tarrant County homes

August 13, 2026 · 6 min read · Fort Worth, TX

Two quotes are sitting on your kitchen table. One says architectural shingles. The other says standing seam metal and is roughly double the number. Both roofers swore theirs was the obvious choice. We install both, so we have no horse in this race, and the truthful answer is that the right roof depends on how long you plan to stay in the house, how you feel about hail, and what your budget looks like today versus over 30 years. Here is the math the way we walk through it at kitchen tables across Tarrant County.

Upfront cost: shingles win, clearly

For a typical North Texas home, a full architectural shingle replacement typically costs a fraction of a comparable metal install, and the gap is significant enough that for many families it settles the question on its own. Metal costs more in material and more in labor, because panel work is slower, more precise, and less forgiving of complicated roof lines. We give ranges only after measuring, and we do not guarantee pricing sight unseen, but the relationship between the two numbers is consistent: metal typically runs roughly two to three times the upfront cost of quality shingles on the same house.

Lifespan: metal wins, clearly

Composition shingles in our climate typically deliver 15 to 25 years of service. The Texas heat cycle is hard on asphalt: hundred-degree Augusts, rapid swings when a fall front drops the temperature 40 degrees overnight, and the constant UV load all dry shingles out faster than in gentler climates. Metal, properly installed, typically runs 40 to 60 years. Over a long enough horizon, one metal roof replaces two or even three shingle roofs, which is the entire financial argument for paying more today.

The break-even question

The math only pays off if you are there to collect it. If you plan to sell within ten years, you will likely fund a premium roof for the next owner while recovering only part of it in sale price. If this is your forever house, the second shingle replacement you never buy is where metal quietly wins.

The hail question, honestly

This is Tarrant County, so hail is not hypothetical. The honest comparison:

  • Shingles bruise and lose granules in significant hail, but repairs and full replacements are straightforward and widely covered under standard policies
  • Metal resists puncture far better, but large hail can cosmetically dent panels, and some insurers exclude cosmetic dents from coverage
  • Class 4 impact-rated shingles split the difference and may qualify you for a premium discount, which is worth asking your agent about

Neither material makes hail a non-event. The question is whether you would rather have a cheaper roof that is simpler to repair, or a tougher roof that may carry dents you learn to live with. Either way, knowing what hail damage looks like and what to check first is worth five minutes of reading before the next spring storm season, because early documentation matters regardless of what is on your roof. The National Weather Service logs every hail event in the area, which helps date the damage. We document what we find; your adjuster decides what it means.

Practical tip: Before choosing, call your insurance agent and ask two questions: does my policy exclude cosmetic metal damage, and does a Class 4 shingle earn a premium discount? Ten minutes on the phone can swing the 30-year math meaningfully in either direction.

Heat, energy, and the August factor

Metal with a reflective finish sheds heat better than dark asphalt, and many homeowners report their upstairs runs noticeably cooler in summer. Attic ventilation and insulation still matter more than the roofing material itself, so a well-vented shingle roof can outperform a poorly vented metal one. If comfort is your driver, fix the attic first, then let the roof material be the bonus. Also worth noting: install pace differs. Shingles go on in a day or two; metal takes longer, and our full write-up on how long a roof replacement takes lays out both schedules honestly.

Maintenance and repairs over the years

No roof is maintenance-free. Shingle roofs typically need pipe boot replacements, occasional wind repairs, and sealant refreshes over their life; the work is quick and nearly any crew can do it. Metal needs less frequent attention, but when it does need work, fewer crews handle it well and panel matching can be harder years later. Small problems on either material are cheap when caught early, which is exactly the kind of thing we handle through roof repair calls in Benbrook all the time.

Our plain recommendation

Staying long term and able to absorb the upfront cost: metal deserves a serious look. Selling within ten years, or working with a tighter budget: quality architectural shingles, possibly Class 4 rated, are the sensible answer, and there is nothing second-rate about that choice. Whichever way you lean, get both numbers measured on your actual roof, not estimated from the street.

Common questions

Is a metal roof loud when it rains?
Not on a modern install. Metal over solid decking and underlayment sounds much like any other roof. The loud-rain reputation comes from open-frame barns and patio covers.
Can metal go over my existing shingles?
Sometimes it is technically possible, but we generally recommend a full tear-off so we can inspect and repair the decking. Covering unknown problems with a 50-year roof is a bet we do not like.
Do Class 4 shingles really hold up to hail?
They resist impact meaningfully better than standard shingles in testing and in what we see on roofs after storms. They are not hail-proof, and very large hail can damage any roofing material.

We will measure, walk you through both options, and give you honest ranges with zero pressure.

5 signs your roof needs attention before fall storm season

August 3, 2026 · 6 min read · Fort Worth, TX

It is a Saturday morning in late August, 96 degrees by 10 am, and the last thing on your mind is your roof. That is exactly the problem. North Texas gets a second storm season that catches people flat-footed every year: everyone plans for the spring hail window that the National Weather Service office in Fort Worth tracks every year, but October and November bring their own fronts, with straight-line winds pushing across the Cross Timbers, sideways rain, and the occasional late-season hail core. The roofs that leak in those storms almost always telegraphed it weeks earlier. Here are the five signs we look for, most of which you can check yourself from the ground this weekend.

1. Granules collecting where they should not

Check the splash blocks and the ground below your downspouts. Granules protect the asphalt in your shingles from UV, and a summer of Texas sun accelerates the shedding on any roof that is already tired. Light, occasional grit is normal on an aging roof. Steady accumulation, or bald patches you can see from the yard, means the shingles are burning through their remaining life quickly. If the shedding started right after a spring storm, it is also worth reviewing what hail damage looks like from the ground, because granule loss is one of the primary hail signatures and the two problems often overlap.

2. Lifted, curled, or wavy shingle edges

Walk the perimeter of your house and sight along each roof plane like you would sight down a board. Shingle edges that curl up or wave instead of lying flat have lost their seal, and an unsealed shingle is exactly what a 50 mph October gust peels off. The fix for a few unsealed shingles is quick and cheap in September. In November, after the wind finds them, it is a leak, a stain, and an interior repair.

3. Flashing and pipe boots that summer cooked

The rubber boots around your plumbing vents typically fail years before the shingles around them. Texas sun cracks the rubber, and a cracked boot is one of the most common leak sources we repair. From the ground with binoculars, or from a ladder at the eave, look for:

  • Cracked or split rubber around vent pipes
  • Flashing pulling away from chimneys or walls
  • Rusted or lifted metal in the valleys
  • Ridge cap shingles that look cracked or loose

These small penetration failures cause an outsized share of the leak calls we run, and they are also the cheapest items on this list to fix. Most of the roof repairs in Benbrook we handle in a typical fall are exactly this category: an hour or two of work that prevents a ceiling repair.

4. Ceiling and attic clues inside the house

The five-minute attic check

Pick a bright afternoon and spend five minutes in the attic with the lights off. Pinpoints of daylight through the decking mean open nail holes or gaps that wind-driven rain will find. While you are up there, look for water staining on the decking, rusted nail tips, and insulation that looks matted or discolored in one spot. Inside the house, a faint tan ring on a ceiling, even one that seems old and dry, is a record that water has already found a path at least once. Fall storms are how old paths become active ones.

5. A roof that has quietly hit its age

If your composition roof is past 15 years in this climate, it deserves a professional look before every storm season, even with none of the symptoms above. Heat-cycled asphalt loses flexibility with age, and an older roof can go from serviceable to vulnerable in a single summer. An honest inspection either buys you another season of confidence or catches the decline while your options are still open. If the verdict is that the roof is near the end, it helps to understand how long a replacement actually takes so you can plan the project on your calendar instead of the weather's.

Practical tip: Book inspections in late August or September. After the first big fall front, every roofer in DFW is running weeks out. Before it, you can usually get an inspection within days and any small repairs finished ahead of the weather.

What a pre-season inspection actually covers

A real inspection is not a guy glancing from the driveway. We walk every slope, check the ridge and valleys, test the penetrations, inspect the flashing details, and look in the attic when there is any sign of moisture. Everything gets photographed, and you get a written summary that says one of three things: the roof is ready, the roof needs specific small repairs, or the roof has larger problems worth discussing. Most fall inspections land in the first two categories. We run these across the north side of the metro as well, including storm inspections in Saginaw, where the fall wind exposure off open land tends to find loose shingles first.

Twenty minutes of ground-level checks this weekend, and one professional inspection before the first front, is the whole program. It is the cheapest insurance the fall season offers. For the rest of the house, ready.gov's severe weather guide is a solid checklist.

Common questions

Is a roof inspection worth it if I have no leaks?
Yes. Almost every leak we repair started as a small, visible defect that would have cost far less to fix earlier. An inspection either buys peace of mind or catches a cheap repair before it becomes an expensive one.
Can I just inspect the roof myself?
The ground-level and attic checks above are safe and genuinely useful. We do not recommend homeowners walk their own roofs. Beyond the fall risk, walking a heat-softened shingle roof can cause damage of its own.
What do small repairs before storm season usually involve?
Most commonly pipe boot replacements, resealing exposed nail heads, re-securing loose shingles, and minor flashing work. These are typically quick, inexpensive visits, and they close off the exact entry points fall storms exploit.

Get ahead of fall storm season

Schedule a free pre-season inspection and go into October knowing exactly where your roof stands.

Serving Benbrook, TX

Roof repair in Benbrook TX

Summit Ridge Roofing · Licensed and insured · Tarrant County

Benbrook roofs take a beating from two directions: lake-driven wind coming off Benbrook Lake and the straight-line gusts that roll down the US 377 corridor. Many of the homes here, especially the older ranch-style houses off 377 and around Whitestone Ranch, are on their second or third shingle layer of life, with original decking underneath. That combination means small problems like a lifted shingle, a cracked pipe boot, or a rusted valley can turn into attic leaks fast. Our repair crews work in Benbrook weekly, and most of what we fix is exactly that kind of small, catchable damage.

Common questions in Benbrook

How do I know if I need a repair or a full replacement?
Age and spread. A roof under 15 years old with localized damage is usually a repair. If damage covers multiple slopes or the shingles are brittle across the whole roof, replacement often makes more sense. We show you photos of both scenarios so the call is easy to make.
My ceiling stain is nowhere near the roof damage I can see. Is that normal?
Very. Water travels along decking and rafters before it drops, so the stain and the entry point are often rooms apart. That is why we trace leaks from the roof down instead of guessing from the ceiling up.
Will you work with my insurance if the damage came from a storm?
We document the damage thoroughly with photos and a written report you can hand to your carrier. Your adjuster makes the call on coverage. We never promise an outcome, but good documentation makes the process much smoother.

Common questions in White Settlement

How long does a replacement take on an older home?
Most single-family replacements here finish in one to two days. Older homes that need decking work can run a day longer. We confirm the schedule before we start and tell you the same day if tear-off reveals anything that changes it.
Can you roof over my existing shingles to save money?
We do not recommend it, and on many older White Settlement homes there are already multiple layers, which makes an overlay a bad idea structurally and for resale. A full tear-off lets us actually see and fix the decking, which is where older roofs hide their problems.
The jets from the base rattle my house. Does that affect my roof?
Vibration alone will not wear out shingles, but it can loosen fasteners on flashing and vents that were marginal to begin with. It is one more reason we re-flash everything during a replacement instead of reusing old metal.

Common questions in Saginaw

My roof looks fine from the street. Should I still get it inspected after hail?
Yes, especially on newer roofs in areas like Willow Creek and Highland Station. Hail bruising on asphalt shingles is often invisible from the ground but shortens shingle life by knocking granules loose. An inspection either finds it or gives you documented peace of mind.
How soon after a storm should I schedule an inspection?
Within a couple of weeks is ideal. Damage does not get better with time, and if you have an active leak, sooner protects your decking and interior. Most carriers also have time limits on storm claims, so early documentation keeps your options open.
Will you tell my insurance company what to pay?
No, and be wary of anyone who promises that. We document the damage with photos and a written report, and your adjuster makes the coverage call. Our job is to make sure nothing real gets missed and nothing gets exaggerated.
